keyVerseText: When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay, anointed: or, spread the clay upon the eyes of the blind man
rootMeaning: The Greek noun πηλός (pēlós) fundamentally denotes 'clay,' a natural earthy substance used by potters and masons. While its precise etymology is uncertain, it appears to be a primary word in Greek, emphasizing the tangible, malleable material from which objects—and metaphorically, humans—are formed. This root sense of pliable earth enriches the English gloss 'clay' by highlighting the creative and formative potential inherent in the substance, not merely its physicality.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, πηλός occurs six times and is predominantly translated as 'clay,' consistent across four instances, with one occurrence as 'the clay' and another as 'over the clay.' This consistency underscores its role as a concrete substance, often connected to the imagery of human formation and the earth itself. The word also carries metaphorical nuances, such as representing mud or mire, and in some poetic contexts, it relates to thick or muddy wine, revealing a semantic range tied to earthiness and imperfection.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, πηλός draws attention to humanity's origin from the earth, affirming the biblical truth that God is the Creator who forms man from the dust (or clay) of the ground. This word reminds believers of human dependence on God's sovereign shaping and sustaining power, as well as the humility inherent in our earthly nature. It also speaks to God's mastery as the divine Potter who can mold and transform flawed clay into vessels of honor. Recognizing this original meaning enriches our understanding of human identity and divine grace within Scripture.
keyVerseReflection: In John 9:6, Jesus 'spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay.' Here, πηλός is not merely dirt but a deliberate, crafted substance used by Christ in the healing act. The word underscores the tangible, earthly means by which Jesus brings spiritual and physical restoration, symbolizing God's power to transform what is humble and common into an instrument of miraculous grace.
